title: Conservatives and Liberals
q: A statesman argues that hereditary monarchy, an established church, and traditional social ranks are necessary barriers against revolutionary chaos. Which ideology best matches his position?
opts: Conservatism
Liberalism
Nationalism
Socialism
explanation: Conservatives defended inherited institutions, social hierarchy, monarchy, and organized religion because they associated rapid change with the violence of the French Revolution. Liberals favored constitutions and individual rights; nationalists emphasized shared identity and statehood; socialists focused on economic class and ownership.

title: Liberal Goals
q: Which reform would a European liberal of the early 1800s be most likely to support?
opts: Restoring unlimited royal authority
Giving aristocrats permanent control of legislatures
A written constitution protecting civil liberties and limiting government power
Suppressing newspapers that criticize the monarch
explanation: Nineteenth-century liberals generally supported constitutional government, equality before the law, private property, religious toleration, and freedom of speech and press. Unlimited monarchy, aristocratic privilege, and censorship were conservative policies liberals opposed.

title: Conservative and Liberal Beliefs
q: Which positions were commonly associated with nineteenth-century liberalism? Select all that apply.
correct: Civil liberties such as freedom of speech and press
opts: Government based on a constitution
Civil liberties such as freedom of speech and press
Equality before the law
Restoration of feudal privileges
Permanent censorship of political criticism
explanation: Liberals sought constitutional limits, civil liberties, and legal equality. Feudal privilege and permanent censorship protected the old order and therefore aligned more closely with conservatism.

title: Nationalism
q: People who share a language, culture, history, and traditions demand that scattered territories be united under one government. Their demand is primarily an expression of:
opts: Absolutism
Nationalism
Mercantilism
Laissez-faire economics
explanation: Nationalism holds that people joined by a common identity should form or control their own political state. Absolutism concerns royal power, mercantilism concerns state-regulated trade, and laissez-faire concerns limited economic regulation.

title: Nationalism as a Force
q: Why could nationalism both unify and divide nineteenth-century Europe?
opts: It always strengthened multinational empires
It concerned only economic policy
It rejected common language and culture
It united culturally related peoples while encouraging minorities inside empires to seek independence
explanation: Nationalism helped unite Germany and Italy, but it also weakened the Austrian and Ottoman empires by inspiring subject peoples to demand autonomy or statehood. Its effect depended on whether a national group was politically divided or trapped inside a multinational empire.

title: Congress of Vienna
q: What was the central goal of the Congress of Vienna after Napoleon's defeat?
opts: Restore stability through legitimacy and a balance of power
Create democratic republics throughout Europe
Unify Germany and Italy immediately
Abolish all European monarchies
explanation: The Congress sought stability by restoring legitimate dynasties, containing France, and balancing the great powers so no state could dominate Europe. It was conservative and did not aim to spread republics or national unification.

title: Metternich and the Vienna Settlement
q: Klemens von Metternich would most likely view liberal and nationalist movements as dangerous because they:
opts: Guaranteed Austrian control of Europe
Protected every traditional dynasty
Threatened monarchies and the unity of multinational empires
Prevented citizens from demanding constitutions
explanation: As an Austrian conservative, Metternich feared that constitutional demands would weaken rulers and nationalism would tear apart the Habsburg Empire's many ethnic groups. The movements undermined rather than protected the old order.

title: Vienna Settlement Methods
q: Which actions reflected the Congress of Vienna's conservative settlement? Select all that apply.
correct: Creating a balance among the great powers
opts: Restoring displaced royal dynasties
Strengthening states around France
Creating a balance among the great powers
Granting universal suffrage across Europe
Recognizing every ethnic group's independent state
explanation: Restoration, containment, and balance of power were core Vienna principles. Universal suffrage and national self-determination would have challenged the monarchies and borders the delegates were trying to preserve.

title: Serbian and Greek Independence
q: The Serbian and Greek revolts were similar because both movements:
opts: Sought independence from Austria
Challenged Ottoman rule through nationalism
Restored French control in the Balkans
Opposed the idea of cultural identity
explanation: Both Serbs and Greeks used national identity to resist Ottoman authority. Serbia gained substantial autonomy after revolts beginning in 1804, and Greece won recognized independence in 1830.

title: Belgian Revolution
q: Which combination best explains Belgium's successful revolt against Dutch rule in 1830?
opts: Identical religions and equal representation
A desire to join the Ottoman Empire
Religious differences, inadequate representation, and inspiration from France
Prussian occupation and Russian military aid
explanation: Catholic Belgians resented rule by the largely Protestant Dutch and felt politically and economically neglected. The French July Revolution showed that a government could be overthrown, encouraging Belgian action.

title: France after Napoleon
q: Why did Louis XVIII face opposition after being restored to the French throne?
opts: He abolished monarchy immediately
He refused any charter or legislature
France had no ideological divisions after 1815
His constitutional compromise satisfied neither hard-line royalists nor liberals
explanation: Louis XVIII accepted the Charter of French Liberties, attempting to combine monarchy with limited constitutionalism. Ultra-royalists thought he conceded too much, while liberals believed the settlement did not protect enough rights or participation.

title: July Revolution
q: What most directly caused Charles X to lose the French throne in the July Revolution of 1830?
opts: His attempt to restore stronger absolute rule and restrict liberties
His support for universal male suffrage
His alliance with radical socialists
His decision to close the Catholic Church
explanation: Charles X's reactionary policies and July Ordinances restricted the press and political participation, provoking revolt. He abdicated, and Louis-Philippe became the constitutional 'Citizen King.'

title: Causes of the 1848 French Revolution
q: Which conditions contributed to revolution in France in February 1848? Select all that apply.
correct: Government corruption and repression of protest
opts: Economic recession and factory closures
Food shortages
Government corruption and repression of protest
A period of universal prosperity
Louis-Philippe's successful expansion of voting rights to all adults
explanation: Recession, unemployment, food scarcity, corruption, and the government's violent response to protest destroyed support for Louis-Philippe. Prosperity and universal voting rights did not characterize his government.

title: Second Republic
q: What was France's Second Republic?
opts: The absolute monarchy of Charles X
The republican government created after Louis-Philippe abdicated in 1848
Napoleon III's empire after 1852
The government formed after the Franco-Prussian War
explanation: The February Revolution of 1848 ended Louis-Philippe's monarchy and produced the Second Republic. It was later destroyed when Louis-Napoleon staged a coup and became Emperor Napoleon III.

title: June Days
q: The June Days uprising of 1848 revealed which major division inside the new French republic?
opts: A conflict between France and Britain
A religious war between Catholics and Protestants
Class conflict between workers and the middle- and upper-class government
A dispute over restoring feudal serfdom
explanation: Workers rebelled after the government closed the National Workshops that had provided employment. The violent suppression, which killed about 1,500 citizens, exposed the republic's sharp class divisions.

title: Louis-Napoleon
q: How did Louis-Napoleon transform the Second Republic?
opts: He surrendered power to the National Assembly
He restored Louis-Philippe
He made France a British colony
He used a coup to dissolve republican government and became Napoleon III
explanation: Elected president in 1848, Louis-Napoleon later dissolved the National Assembly in a coup and established authoritarian rule, becoming Emperor Napoleon III. His rise ended the Second Republic.

title: Revolutions of 1848
q: Why did many European revolutions of 1848 fail despite early successes?
opts: Revolutionaries were divided, and conservative armies recovered and reasserted control
All monarchs voluntarily accepted national self-determination
Workers and middle-class liberals agreed on every goal
Foreign powers refused to aid conservative governments
explanation: Liberal, nationalist, and working-class revolutionaries often wanted different outcomes. Once frightened elites regrouped, loyal armies and foreign intervention restored conservative control in Austria, Italy, and much of Germany.

title: Frankfurt Assembly
q: Why did Frederick William IV's rejection of a crown offered by the Frankfurt Assembly damage the cause of German unity in 1848?
opts: It gave Austria permanent control of France
It showed that liberal nationalists lacked the military power to make a king accept their constitution
It immediately unified Germany under republican rule
It ended Prussia's existence
explanation: The Frankfurt Assembly depended on voluntary cooperation from established rulers. Frederick William's refusal demonstrated that speeches and constitutions alone could not overcome monarchical and military power.

title: Atlantic Revolutions
q: Which two broad conditions encouraged independence movements in Latin America?
opts: The decline of Enlightenment ideas and stronger Spanish control
Industrialization and Ottoman conquest
Enlightenment ideas and political chaos in Europe
The Congress of Vienna's support for colonial independence
explanation: Ideas of natural rights and popular sovereignty crossed the Atlantic, while Napoleon's invasions disrupted Spain and Portugal. Colonial elites and other groups used the crisis to challenge imperial authority.

title: Haitian Revolution
q: Why was the Haitian Revolution historically unique?
opts: It was the only large-scale slave revolt to create an independent nation
It preserved slavery under a French governor
It established the first European monarchy in the Americas
It succeeded without warfare
explanation: Enslaved people in Saint-Domingue defeated major imperial armies and created independent Haiti in 1804. The revolution directly challenged slavery, colonialism, and racial hierarchy in a way unmatched by other Atlantic revolutions.

title: Toussaint L'Ouverture
q: What best explains Toussaint L'Ouverture's success as a revolutionary leader?
opts: He depended entirely on permanent French military support
He built a disciplined army and skillfully shifted alliances among competing empires
He avoided governing the colony
He restored plantation slavery to gain popular support
explanation: Toussaint combined military organization, political leadership, and flexible diplomacy while French, Spanish, and British forces competed in the Caribbean. Although Napoleon captured him, the movement he helped build survived and won independence.

title: Haitian Revolution Outcomes
q: Which were consequences or historical meanings of the Haitian Revolution? Select all that apply.
opts: Haiti became independent from France
The revolution challenged Atlantic slavery
Slaveholding societies feared similar uprisings
France strengthened slavery permanently in Haiti
Spain peacefully inherited Saint-Domingue
explanation: Haitian independence destroyed slavery in the colony and frightened slaveholding elites throughout the Atlantic world. France did not retain Haiti, and Spain did not inherit it.

title: Mexican Independence
q: Which sequence best describes Mexico's path to independence?
opts: Bolivar invaded Mexico and crowned Hidalgo
Spain granted independence before any revolt
Toussaint defeated the Spanish army in Mexico City
Hidalgo began a mass revolt in 1810, and Iturbide later completed independence through the Plan of Iguala
explanation: Father Miguel Hidalgo launched the 1810 rebellion but was captured and executed. After years of conflict, conservative Creole officer Agustin de Iturbide joined the independence cause and secured separation from Spain in 1821.

title: Hidalgo's Movement
q: Why did many wealthy Creoles initially fear Miguel Hidalgo's independence movement?
opts: It promised to restore Spanish taxes
It was led exclusively by Spanish officials
Its mass support among Indigenous people and mestizos threatened the colonial social order
It demanded that Mexico join Haiti
explanation: Hidalgo mobilized poor and racially marginalized groups, making elites fear social revolution as well as political separation. This helps explain why Mexican independence eventually succeeded through an alliance that protected elite interests.

title: Simon Bolivar
q: Which description best identifies Simon Bolivar?
opts: A Creole leader who helped liberate northern South America from Spanish rule
A Spanish king who reconquered Haiti
An Austrian diplomat who designed the Congress of Vienna
A Mexican priest who issued the Grito de Dolores
explanation: Bolivar, known as El Libertador, led campaigns that helped free Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, and Bolivia. Hidalgo issued the Grito de Dolores; Metternich was the Austrian diplomat.

title: Gran Colombia
q: Why did Bolivar's dream of a durable, united Gran Colombia fail?
opts: Spain immediately reconquered all of South America
Regional rivalries, geography, and competing local elites encouraged fragmentation
Bolivar opposed independence
The United States annexed the entire region
explanation: Mountains and distance complicated government, while regional caudillos and local elites resisted centralized authority. Gran Colombia broke into separate states even though Spain did not reconquer them.

title: Latin American Independence
q: Which factors limited unity and stability after Latin American independence? Select all that apply.
opts: Regional rivalries among local leaders
Difficult geography and weak transportation
Persistent social and ethnic inequality
Complete agreement over centralized government
The disappearance of elite landownership
explanation: Caudillo rivalry, geographic barriers, and inherited inequality made unified government difficult. Independence did not erase elite landownership or create consensus about political structure.

title: German Confederation
q: What was the German Confederation created after the Napoleonic Wars?
opts: A democratic nation led by Prussia
A colony controlled by France
A weak association of German states dominated by Austria
A military union between Germany and Italy
explanation: The Congress of Vienna replaced Napoleon's arrangements with a loose confederation of 39 states. Metternich favored its weakness because Austrian influence and conservative rulers would be safer than in a strong united Germany.

title: Bismarck's Background
q: Bismarck's identity as a Prussian Junker meant that he came from:
opts: The urban socialist working class
The Catholic clergy
A French republican family
The conservative landowning nobility
explanation: Junkers were Prussian landed nobles who traditionally supported the monarchy and army. Bismarck's background helps explain his conservatism and loyalty to Prussian power.

title: Realpolitik
q: What did Bismarck's mastery of Realpolitik involve?
opts: Using practical power calculations rather than fixed ideals
Submitting every policy to popular referendum
Rejecting diplomacy and war under all circumstances
Making religious doctrine the sole basis of foreign policy
explanation: Realpolitik emphasized achievable results, military strength, strategic alliances, and calculated compromise. Bismarck could cooperate with one state and later oppose it if Prussian interests changed.

title: Blood and Iron
q: Bismarck's 'blood and iron' speech most clearly expressed his belief that German unification would be achieved through:
opts: Literary nationalism alone
Military power and decisive state action
Austrian leadership
A workers' revolution
explanation: Bismarck argued that the major questions of the age would not be settled by speeches and parliamentary votes alone. He strengthened the Prussian army and used limited wars to reshape Germany.

title: Wars of German Unification
q: Which conflicts did Bismarck use to expand Prussian power and unify Germany? Select all that apply.
opts: War against Denmark
Austro-Prussian War
Franco-Prussian War
Crimean War against Russia
Greek War of Independence
explanation: The Danish, Austro-Prussian, and Franco-Prussian wars isolated opponents and rallied German states behind Prussia. The Crimean and Greek wars were not stages of Bismarck's unification strategy.

title: Austro-Prussian War
q: What was the most important political result of Prussia's rapid victory over Austria in 1866?
opts: Austria annexed Prussia
France took control of the German states
Austria was excluded from German affairs, allowing Prussia to lead northern Germany
The German Confederation became stronger under Metternich
explanation: The Seven Weeks' War ended Austrian leadership in Germany and allowed Prussia to organize the North German Confederation. This established the foundation for a Prussian-led nation-state.

title: Ems Dispatch
q: Why did Bismarck edit and publish the Ems Dispatch in 1870?
opts: To prevent any conflict with France
To invite Austria back into German leadership
To announce Prussia's surrender
To provoke French outrage and unite German states against a common enemy
explanation: Bismarck shortened the diplomatic report so both France and Prussia appeared insulted. France declared war, and the southern German states joined Prussia, completing national unification after victory.

title: German Constitution
q: How did the constitution of the new German Empire combine popular participation with elite control?
opts: The Reichstag was elected by universal male suffrage, but the Bundesrat and chancellor limited its power
Both houses were elected by women and men
The emperor served only as a powerless symbol
The Reichstag could remove the emperor by simple vote
explanation: Adult men elected the Reichstag, but the Bundesrat represented state rulers and could block it. The emperor appointed the chancellor, so executive and aristocratic power remained strong despite elections.

title: German Industrial Growth
q: Which factors helped unified Germany become an industrial giant? Select all that apply.
correct: Large supplies of coal and iron
A single currency and unified banking system
Industrial investment and a disciplined workforce
opts: Large supplies of coal and iron
A single currency and unified banking system
Industrial investment and a disciplined workforce
Rapid population growth
A ban on factories and railroads
explanation: Natural resources, financial unity, investment, labor, and population growth encouraged rapid industrialization. A ban on factories and railroads would have prevented rather than accelerated growth.

title: Bismarck's Foreign Policy
q: After unification, Bismarck's primary foreign-policy strategy was to:
opts: Prepare an immediate invasion of Britain
Keep France isolated while maintaining workable ties with Austria and Russia
Break Germany into independent states
Build an anti-German alliance with France
explanation: Bismarck regarded satisfied, secure Germany as needing peace. He tried to prevent France from finding allies and managed relations among Austria and Russia to avoid a two-front war.

title: Kulturkampf
q: Bismarck's Kulturkampf was an effort to:
opts: Unify Germany with France
Expand the authority of the pope in Germany
Reduce Catholic Church influence and strengthen state loyalty
End all public education
explanation: Bismarck feared that Catholics might place loyalty to the pope above loyalty to the empire. His campaign restricted Church influence, although resistance eventually forced him to retreat from several measures.

title: William II and Bismarck
q: Why did Kaiser William II remove Bismarck from power?
opts: Bismarck supported French control of Germany
The Reichstag legally abolished the chancellorship
Bismarck refused to serve William I
The young emperor wanted to rule personally and disagreed with the older chancellor's policies
explanation: William II declared that there would be only one master in the Reich. Personal rivalry and policy disagreements led him to demand Bismarck's resignation in 1890.

title: William II's Germany
q: Which policy most clearly distinguished William II from Bismarck?
opts: A major naval buildup intended to rival Britain
Permanent avoidance of overseas competition
Restoration of the German Confederation
Elimination of all social welfare programs
explanation: William II pursued a more aggressive world policy and greatly expanded the navy, alarming Britain. He also adopted some welfare measures, so eliminating all social programs is incorrect.

title: Mazzini and Young Italy
q: What was Giuseppe Mazzini's contribution to Italian unification?
opts: He defended Austrian rule
He founded Young Italy and promoted a united nation based on common heritage
He served as pope and opposed nationalism
He commanded the Prussian army
explanation: Mazzini supplied ideological inspiration through Young Italy, arguing that Italians shared a historical and cultural identity. His revolts often failed, but his nationalism shaped later unification.

title: Cavour's Strategy
q: Why did Cavour bring Sardinia-Piedmont into the Crimean War?
opts: To conquer Russia permanently
To support Austrian control of Italy
To gain diplomatic influence with Britain and France for the Italian cause
To help Garibaldi become king of France
explanation: Sardinia's military contribution was small, but participation earned Cavour a place at the peace talks. He used that visibility to win support, especially from Napoleon III, against Austria.

title: Cavour and Garibaldi
q: Which statement best contrasts Cavour and Garibaldi?
opts: Both relied only on peaceful petitions
Garibaldi was a diplomat, while Cavour led the Red Shirts
Both wanted Italy permanently divided
Cavour used diplomacy and monarchy in the north, while Garibaldi used volunteer warfare in the south
explanation: Cavour directed Sardinia-Piedmont's statecraft and alliances. Garibaldi and his Red Shirts conquered Sicily and Naples, then transferred those lands to Victor Emmanuel II.

title: Italian Unification Leaders
q: Which leader-role pairings are accurate? Select all that apply.
correct: Mazzini - nationalist founder of Young Italy
Cavour - Sardinian prime minister and diplomat
Garibaldi - commander of the Red Shirts
Victor Emmanuel II - monarch of unified Italy
opts: Mazzini - nationalist founder of Young Italy
Cavour - Sardinian prime minister and diplomat
Garibaldi - commander of the Red Shirts
Victor Emmanuel II - monarch of unified Italy
Metternich - leader of the Red Shirts
explanation: Mazzini inspired, Cavour maneuvered diplomatically, Garibaldi conquered in the south, and Victor Emmanuel II became king. Metternich was an Austrian conservative who opposed Italian nationalism.

title: Foreign Powers and Italy
q: How did foreign affairs assist Italian unification?
opts: French aid helped Sardinia fight Austria, and later European wars distracted troops holding Italian territory
Austria voluntarily united Italy
Russia conquered and transferred all Italian states
Britain installed Garibaldi as emperor
explanation: Cavour secured Napoleon III's assistance against Austria. Later, the Austro-Prussian and Franco-Prussian wars created opportunities for Italy to gain Venetia and Rome.

title: Problems of Unified Italy
q: Which problems confronted Italy after unification? Select all that apply.
opts: Regional languages and identities
Conflict with the papacy
Political turmoil and socialist growth
Uneven industrialization and mass emigration
Complete economic equality between north and south
explanation: Political borders did not instantly create a shared identity or equal economy. Regional division, Church hostility, social conflict, industrial disruption, and migration remained major challenges.

title: Making Italians
q: The statement 'We have made Italy; now we must make Italians' means that:
opts: Italy still lacked legal borders
Political unification had occurred, but a common national identity remained weak
Austria still ruled every Italian state
All Italians already shared identical language and culture
explanation: Many residents identified more strongly with region, town, or dialect than with the new nation. The state therefore had to build common institutions and loyalty after formal unification.

title: Britain's Two Nations
q: In Benjamin Disraeli's description of Britain as 'two nations,' the two groups were:
opts: England and France
Catholics and Protestants
The rich and the poor
Farmers and sailors
explanation: Disraeli emphasized the social separation between wealthy and impoverished Britons created or intensified by industrial society. The phrase highlighted class inequality, not international rivalry.

title: Parliamentary Representation
q: Why were rotten boroughs criticized before the Reform Act of 1832?
opts: They gave industrial cities too many representatives
They elected members by universal suffrage
They were controlled by labor unions
They retained parliamentary seats despite having very few voters
explanation: Tiny or nearly abandoned districts could send members to Parliament, while rapidly growing industrial cities were underrepresented. This made representation unequal and vulnerable to aristocratic control.

title: Reform Act of 1832
q: What did the Reform Act of 1832 accomplish?
opts: It expanded the electorate and redistributed parliamentary representation
It granted women full voting rights
It abolished the House of Commons
It restored rotten boroughs
explanation: The act eliminated many rotten borough seats, gave more representation to industrial areas, and expanded voting among property-owning men. It was important but did not create universal suffrage or enfranchise women.

title: Chartist Demands
q: Which reforms were associated with the Chartist movement? Select all that apply.
opts: Broader male suffrage
Secret ballots
More representative parliamentary districts
Permanent rule by the House of Lords
The abolition of elections
explanation: Chartists demanded a more democratic Parliament, especially for working men. Secret voting and fairer districts would reduce elite control; abolishing elections or strengthening hereditary rule would do the opposite.

title: Victorian Political Reform
q: Which statement best evaluates Victorian parliamentary reform?
opts: Britain immediately became a full democracy in 1832
Voting rights and Commons power expanded gradually, but women and many workers waited decades for full participation
The House of Lords gained unlimited veto power in 1911
Political parties stopped competing
explanation: A series of reforms broadened male suffrage, adopted the secret ballot, and reduced the Lords' power. The process was gradual and incomplete; British women did not gain parliamentary voting rights until 1918.

title: Victorian Ideals
q: Which values were most closely associated with Victorian ideals?
opts: Revolution, idleness, and extravagance
Military dictatorship and censorship
Hard work, thrift, duty, honesty, and loyalty
Rejection of family and religion
explanation: Victorian culture publicly celebrated discipline, responsibility, thrift, honesty, and loyalty. These ideals coexisted with severe class inequality and imperial expansion.

title: Corn Laws
q: Why did industrial and urban interests favor repeal of the Corn Laws?
opts: They wanted imported grain taxed more heavily
They wanted to protect only aristocratic landlords
They opposed all foreign trade
Cheaper imported grain could lower food prices and pressure on wages
explanation: The Corn Laws protected British grain producers with tariffs, keeping food prices high. Manufacturers and urban consumers favored repeal because cheaper food benefited workers and supported free trade.

title: British Social Reforms
q: Which changes represented social or political reform in nineteenth-century Britain? Select all that apply.
correct: Abolition of the slave trade in 1807
Reduction in the number of capital crimes
opts: Abolition of the slave trade in 1807
Abolition of slavery in 1833
Legal expansion of labor unions
Reduction in the number of capital crimes
Restoration of slavery in industrial cities
explanation: Britain ended the slave trade, abolished slavery in most of its empire, reduced harsh criminal penalties, and increasingly recognized unions. Restoring slavery was not a reform.

title: Labour Party
q: The emergence of the Labour Party in 1900 most directly reflected:
opts: The growing political organization of workers seeking social legislation
The disappearance of industrial labor
A campaign to strengthen rotten boroughs
A demand for restored feudalism
explanation: Trade unionists and social reformers wanted direct representation for working-class interests and welfare legislation. Industrial labor had expanded, not disappeared.

title: Irish Grievances
q: Which issues fueled Irish nationalism under British rule? Select all that apply.
correct: Tithes supporting the Church of England
Demands for Catholic emancipation and Home Rule
opts: Absentee landlords
Tithes supporting the Church of England
The Great Hunger
Demands for Catholic emancipation and Home Rule
Equal political and religious treatment from the beginning
explanation: Landlordism, religious discrimination, famine, and limited self-government generated resentment. Daniel O'Connell pursued Catholic emancipation, while later moderates sought Home Rule and radicals pursued independence.

title: Napoleon III's Domestic Rule
q: How did Napoleon III's domestic government change during his reign?
opts: It began democratic and became more absolute every year
It began authoritarian but gradually allowed more political rights in the 1860s
It immediately abolished industrial investment
It placed all power in the Paris Commune
explanation: Napoleon III initially ruled as an authoritarian emperor, restricting opposition. In the 1860s he liberalized parts of the regime, though France did not become a fully parliamentary democracy.

title: Suez Canal
q: What was the purpose of the Suez Canal, and how was France connected to it?
opts: It connected the Atlantic and Pacific and was built by Germany
It linked the Rhine and Danube and was financed only by Britain
It connected the Mediterranean and Red seas and was built by a French-led company
It carried trains across the Alps and was designed by Cavour
explanation: The canal created a much shorter route between Europe and the Indian Ocean. Ferdinand de Lesseps and a French-led company developed it, though Britain later acquired major shares and strategic influence.

title: Napoleon III's Foreign Policy
q: Which statements accurately describe Napoleon III's foreign-policy record? Select all that apply.
correct: He won prestige in the Crimean War but gained little for its cost
He supported Italian nationalists against Austria
His attempt to establish a satellite monarchy in Mexico failed
He was defeated in the Franco-Prussian War
opts: He won prestige in the Crimean War but gained little for its cost
He supported Italian nationalists against Austria
His attempt to establish a satellite monarchy in Mexico failed
He was defeated in the Franco-Prussian War
He permanently annexed Prussia to France
explanation: Napoleon III had mixed early successes, but the Mexican adventure collapsed and the Franco-Prussian War destroyed his empire. France never annexed Prussia.

title: Fall of Napoleon III
q: What event directly ended Napoleon III's rule?
opts: The repeal of the Corn Laws
The Congress of Vienna
The Dreyfus Affair
His capture after the French defeat at Sedan in 1870
explanation: Prussian forces defeated and captured Napoleon III at Sedan during the Franco-Prussian War. The empire collapsed, and France proclaimed the Third Republic.

title: Paris Commune
q: What was the Paris Commune of 1871?
opts: A radical government in Paris that resisted the conservative national government after defeat by Prussia
A Prussian parliament elected by French voters
A royalist movement that restored Napoleon III
A peaceful labor union recognized by Bismarck
explanation: Radicals and socialists in Paris rejected the national government's surrender and authority. Civil war followed, and government troops crushed the Commune during a bloody campaign.

title: Suppression of the Commune
q: What did the suppression of the Paris Commune demonstrate?
opts: France had eliminated class conflict
The Third Republic was willing to use extreme violence against radical urban opposition
Prussia permanently governed Paris
Socialists controlled the French army
explanation: Thousands were killed, arrested, or deported when the army retook Paris. The episode revealed the deep divide between radical workers and the more conservative national government.

title: Third Republic Government
q: Why did coalition governments become common in France's Third Republic?
opts: Only one political party was legal
The president ruled as an absolute monarch
Many parties shared the legislature, so alliances were needed to govern
The army selected every member of parliament
explanation: The Third Republic had a two-house legislature and numerous political parties. Because no single party consistently held a majority, cabinets depended on coalitions led by a premier.

title: Dreyfus Affair
q: Why did the Dreyfus Affair divide French society so deeply?
opts: Dreyfus admitted spying for Germany
The evidence was strong and uncontested
It concerned only a minor tax dispute
A Jewish officer was falsely convicted, exposing antisemitism and conflict over the army and republic
explanation: Forged and concealed evidence kept Alfred Dreyfus imprisoned while nationalists and antisemites defended the military. Supporters demanded justice and civilian accountability, creating a major political and cultural split.

title: Dreyfus and Zionism
q: How did the Dreyfus Affair influence Theodor Herzl?
opts: It convinced him that Jews needed a secure national homeland
It led him to oppose all forms of nationalism
It made him a French military officer
It persuaded him that antisemitism had disappeared
explanation: Herzl saw that even an assimilated Jewish officer in republican France could become a target of antisemitism. He became a leading advocate of political Zionism and a Jewish homeland.

title: Habsburg Nationalities
q: Why was nationalism especially dangerous to the Habsburg Empire?
opts: Nearly everyone in the empire shared one language
The empire ruled many nationalities, while German-speaking Austrians were a minority
Austria had already granted every group independence
Nationalism strengthened Metternich's centralized control
explanation: The Habsburg lands included Hungarians, Czechs, Slovaks, Poles, Italians, Croats, Serbs, Romanians, and others. National demands therefore threatened to fragment the dynasty's multinational state.

title: Francis Joseph
q: How did Francis Joseph initially respond to the revolutions and nationalist pressures facing Austria?
opts: He dissolved the empire voluntarily
He made every nationality fully independent
He consolidated monarchical power while offering limited constitutional change
He placed Garibaldi in charge of Austria
explanation: Francis Joseph became emperor during the crisis of 1848 and restored central authority. Constitutional concessions existed, but power remained concentrated among the monarchy and German-speaking Austrian elites.

title: Dual Monarchy
q: What created the Dual Monarchy of Austria-Hungary in 1867?
opts: Austria's victory over Prussia
Ottoman conquest of Vienna
The unification of Austria and Germany
A compromise after defeat by Prussia that gave Hungary substantial self-government
explanation: Austria's 1866 defeat weakened the monarchy and strengthened Hungarian demands. The Ausgleich created separate Austrian and Hungarian governments under Francis Joseph as emperor and king.

title: Limits of the Dual Monarchy
q: Why did the Dual Monarchy fail to solve Austria-Hungary's nationality problem?
opts: It favored Germans and Magyars while other national groups still lacked comparable autonomy
It gave every ethnic group an independent parliament
It abolished Hungarian political power
It merged the empire into Russia
explanation: The compromise satisfied many Hungarian demands but did not do the same for Czechs, Slovaks, Croats, Serbs, Romanians, and others. These groups continued to seek autonomy or independence.

title: Ottoman Decline
q: Which factors contributed to the Ottoman Empire's decline in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries? Select all that apply.
correct: Military and economic weakness relative to industrial powers
opts: Nationalist revolts among subject peoples
European competition for Ottoman territory
Military and economic weakness relative to industrial powers
A complete absence of foreign interference
Successful permanent control of every Balkan nationality
explanation: Nationalism weakened Ottoman control, while Russia, Austria, Britain, and others competed over Ottoman lands and influence. Industrial and military disadvantages made resistance difficult.

title: Sick Man of Europe
q: Calling the Ottoman Empire the 'sick man of Europe' implied that:
opts: It was Europe's strongest industrial state
It was weakening, and rival powers expected to profit from its decline
It had unified the Balkans through nationalism
It had conquered Russia
explanation: The phrase described the empire's loss of territory and declining ability to resist foreign pressure. European powers disagreed over how to divide influence and prevent rivals from gaining too much.

title: Balkan Wars
q: Why did the Balkan Wars of 1912-1913 make the region a 'powder keg'?
opts: They ended nationalism permanently
They created a stable alliance trusted by every state
Territorial rivalry and nationalism intensified while great powers backed competing interests
They restored complete Ottoman control
explanation: Balkan states fought the Ottomans and then one another over territory. National ambitions, unreliable alliances, and intervention by Austria-Hungary and Russia made a wider war increasingly likely.

title: Russia before Reform
q: Which feature made Russian modernization difficult in the mid-1800s?
opts: A powerful independent middle class
Universal education and broad political rights
The absence of aristocratic landowners
Serfdom, weak middle classes, and autocratic tsarist rule
explanation: Russia remained dominated by nobles and an absolute monarchy, while millions of poor serfs had little mobility or purchasing power. These conditions slowed economic and political modernization.

title: Crimean War and Reform
q: Why did defeat in the Crimean War encourage Alexander II to reform Russia?
opts: It exposed Russia's military, transportation, and administrative weaknesses
It proved serfdom made Russia more advanced than Britain
It gave Russia control of all Ottoman territory
It ended the monarchy immediately
explanation: Defeat by more industrialized powers showed that Russia's social and economic structure weakened its military. Alexander II concluded that reforms were necessary to preserve Russia as a great power.

title: Emancipation of the Serfs
q: What was Alexander II's most famous reform?
opts: Creating the Soviet Union
Emancipating Russia's serfs in 1861
Abolishing the Orthodox Church
Granting independence to every nationality
explanation: Alexander II freed the serfs in 1861. The reform was historic, but many peasants received inadequate land and heavy redemption payments, limiting its economic benefits.

title: Zemstvos
q: What were zemstvos?
opts: Secret police units
Private factories owned by the tsar
Locally elected assemblies responsible for limited self-government
National legislatures able to remove the tsar
explanation: Zemstvos handled local services such as roads, schools, and health. They introduced limited participation but did not replace autocracy or control national policy.

title: Alexander III's Reaction
q: How did Alexander III respond after Alexander II was assassinated?
opts: He expanded revolutionary socialism
He granted a democratic constitution
He ended discrimination against minorities
He tightened autocratic rule and encouraged repression, Russification, and pogroms
explanation: Alexander III reversed much of the reform spirit, strengthened censorship and police power, promoted Russian culture over minorities, and tolerated or encouraged violent antisemitic pogroms.

title: Russian Industrialization
q: Which tensions accompanied Russian industrialization under Alexander III and Nicholas II? Select all that apply.
opts: Harsh urban working conditions
A growing revolutionary labor movement
Continued peasant poverty
Autocratic resistance to political reform
Immediate economic equality for all Russians
explanation: Industrial growth expanded railways and factories but concentrated workers in difficult conditions. Peasant poverty and autocracy continued, creating rather than resolving revolutionary pressures.

title: Russo-Japanese War
q: Why did the Russo-Japanese War intensify Russia's domestic crisis?
opts: Unexpected defeats discredited the tsar and worsened economic hardship
Russia's easy victory made Nicholas II too popular
Japan restored serfdom in Russia
The war gave the Duma complete power
explanation: Defeat by Japan shocked Russians who expected victory and exposed government incompetence. Wartime shortages and frustration contributed directly to the Revolution of 1905.

title: Bloody Sunday
q: Why was Bloody Sunday a turning point in 1905?
opts: Peaceful workers crowned Nicholas II
Troops fired on peaceful petitioners, destroying faith in the tsar as protector
The Duma ordered the army to invade Japan
Alexander II returned to power
explanation: Workers marched peacefully to present grievances, but imperial troops killed and wounded protesters. The massacre triggered strikes, mutinies, and wider opposition to Nicholas II.

title: October Manifesto
q: What did Nicholas II promise in the October Manifesto?
opts: The restoration of serfdom
Immediate abdication
Civil liberties and an elected Duma
Union with Austria-Hungary
explanation: Facing the Revolution of 1905, Nicholas promised basic freedoms and a national legislature. The concession divided the opposition and helped the regime survive temporarily.

title: Limits of the Duma
q: Why did the Duma fail to make Russia a stable constitutional monarchy?
opts: It held unlimited control over the military and budget
It abolished the tsar's office
It refused to meet at all
Nicholas II dissolved critical Dumas and preserved broad autocratic powers
explanation: The tsar accepted a legislature under pressure but did not accept genuine parliamentary control. He dismissed assemblies that challenged him and manipulated election laws.

title: Stolypin
q: What best characterizes Prime Minister Peter Stolypin's approach?
opts: Combining limited agrarian reform with harsh repression of revolutionaries
Ending all police action and distributing equal land
Replacing Nicholas II with an elected president
Restoring Ottoman control of Russia
explanation: Stolypin tried to create prosperous, conservative peasant landowners while using executions, arrests, and censorship against opponents. Reform and repression operated together.

title: Russia on the Eve of World War I
q: Which unresolved problems left Russia unstable by 1914? Select all that apply.
correct: Limited political power for the Duma
Loss of confidence in the tsar
opts: Peasant land hunger and poverty
Poor urban working conditions
Limited political power for the Duma
Ethnic and religious repression
Loss of confidence in the tsar
A fully representative democracy accepted by Nicholas II
explanation: Russia had modernized unevenly without resolving land, labor, nationality, or constitutional questions. Nicholas II's defense of autocracy meant these pressures remained active when war began.

title: Comparing Unification
q: What was one major similarity between German and Italian unification?
opts: Both occurred without war or foreign diplomacy
Both combined nationalist feeling with leadership by an existing kingdom
Both created democratic republics immediately
Both were led by Metternich
explanation: Prussia led German unification, while Sardinia-Piedmont led Italian unification. In both cases, nationalism mattered, but established monarchies, armies, and diplomatic leaders converted sentiment into state power.

title: Comparing Bismarck and Cavour
q: How were Bismarck and Cavour most alike?
opts: Both were radical republicans
Both rejected alliances with foreign powers
Both used pragmatic diplomacy and limited wars to strengthen their monarchies and achieve unification
Both wanted Austria to control their nations
explanation: Neither leader was primarily an idealistic democrat. Bismarck served Prussia and Cavour served Sardinia-Piedmont, using alliances, calculation, and war to expand their states.

title: Revolution and Reform
q: Which broad pattern best describes political change in nineteenth-century Europe?
opts: Every revolution succeeded immediately
Conservatives prevented all reform
Nationalism affected only France
Even failed revolutions pressured governments toward gradual reform while nationalism reshaped borders
explanation: Many uprisings were crushed, but their demands did not disappear. Britain reformed gradually, France repeatedly changed regimes, Germany and Italy unified, and multinational empires faced growing national challenges.

title: Nationalism and Empire
q: Which examples show nationalism weakening multinational empires? Select all that apply.
correct: Hungarian demands within the Habsburg Empire
opts: Greek resistance to Ottoman rule
Hungarian demands within the Habsburg Empire
Balkan movements against Ottoman control
Slavic demands inside Austria-Hungary
British repeal of the Corn Laws
explanation: Each correct example involved a national group challenging rule by a larger multinational empire. Repeal of the Corn Laws was an economic and parliamentary reform, not a nationalist revolt.

title: Nationalism and State Power
q: Which conclusion is best supported by the unifications of Germany and Italy?
opts: National ideals were most successful when joined to armies, diplomacy, and existing state institutions
Poets and students alone could always defeat major empires
Popular elections were the only force behind unification
Foreign wars prevented national unity
explanation: Mazzini and liberal nationalists inspired movements, but Cavour, Garibaldi, Bismarck, monarchs, armies, and international conflicts produced durable states. Ideas mattered most when connected to organized power.
